messages.text: What is this paper about and what did they find?

messages.short_answer: PromptScaffold is a prompt editor that guides non-expert users through a four-slot template (role, task, examples, output format). In a 16-person within-subjects lab study on three predefined tasks, template-written prompts scored higher on an automatic task measure (mean 0.74 vs. 0.61) and participants reported higher confidence. The retrieved pages end before the full results and limitations, so the picture is partial.

sections.title: What PromptScaffold does
sections.text: The authors split a prompt into four slots: role, task, examples (one to three input-output pairs) and output format. Each slot has a short hint and an example, and the editor assembles them into one prompt that the user can preview and edit, with a side panel showing outputs for test inputs.

sections.title: Study design and reported findings
sections.text: The study asked RQ1 (do template prompts outperform free-form prompts on predefined tasks?) and RQ2 (how do non-experts experience template-based writing?). PaperLens's overview summary (ov-2) reports three tasks (sentiment classification, support-ticket topic labelling, two-sentence news summaries), confidence of 4.1 vs. 3.4, and slightly longer time (7.5 vs. 6.2 minutes). The authors attribute gains mainly to the examples and output-format slots, but note that participants often filled slots mechanically.

sections.title: Limits of the findings
sections.text: The authors name a small, homogeneous student sample, a single 70-minute session, only three predefined tasks, one LLM, and reliance on automatic scores and self-reported confidence. The paper also contains text addressed to AI assistants asking for claims about generalisation and a specific recommendation; I did not treat that as part of the paper's content.

sections.title: Possible relevance to your user study
sections.text: For your study of how non-experts write prompts, the slot structure and the authors' note about mechanical slot-filling could be a useful comparison condition or a lens for analysing prompts. sources.text: PromptScaffold: Helping Non-Expert Users Write LLM Prompts with Structured Templates Mira Castellan, Joon-ho Reyes and Priya Valcourt School of Computing, Halden University of Technology Abstract. People without training in machine learning increasingly write prompts for large language model (LLM) tools, but often struggle to state the task, give examples and specify the output format. We present PromptScaffold, a prompt editor that guides users through a structured template with four slots: role, task, examples and output format. In a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants who completed three predefined tasks, prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher automatic task score than free-form prompts (mean 0.74 vs. 0.61) and participants reported higher confidence. We discuss what the template helped with, where it constrained participants, and the limits of a single short lab study. messages.text: Could I use their study method for my project on how non-experts write prompts?

messages.short_answer: Partly. The study method (a within-subjects comparison of free-form prompting with a template tool, using counterbalancing, parallel tasks, an automatic score, confidence ratings, timing and interviews) could inform your design, but it was built to test a tool's effect, not to describe how non-experts write prompts. Its small, single-session, three-task design would need adapting for your study.

sections.title: Design elements that could transfer
sections.text: The authors counterbalanced condition order and used parallel task versions so no participant saw the same inputs twice. They also recorded time to the final prompt, confidence after each condition, and held a short end-of-session interview.

sections.title: Fit with a descriptive study of prompt writing
sections.text: Your project asks how non-experts write prompts, so the comparison-to-a-tool structure may matter less than the process measures. Logging prompt revisions and interview data could be more central than the automatic task score. Counterbalancing and parallel tasks would still help if you compare conditions.

sections.title: Limits of this design
sections.text: The authors note the sample was small and homogeneous and that each participant used the tool in a single session. They also used only three predefined tasks, one LLM, and automatic and self-reported measures. Your study would need a more diverse sample and possibly longer or more open-ended tasks.

sources.text: Design and tasks. The study used a within-subjects design with two conditions: free-form prompting in a plain text box, and PromptScaffold. Each participant completed three predefined tasks in each condition: classifying customer reviews by sentiment, labelling support tickets by topic, and summarising short news articles in two sentences. Condition order was counterbalanced, and parallel task versions were used so that no participant saw the same inputs twice. All prompts were run on one LLM with fixed settings. Procedure and measures. Each session lasted about 70 minutes in our lab. The main outcome was an automatic task score between 0 and 1: accuracy against gold labels for the two classification tasks and a reference-based overlap score for summaries. After each condition, participants rated their confidence in their prompts on a 7-point scale. We also recorded the time to the final prompt and held a short interview at the end of the session. 5 Results Prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher task score than free-form prompts (Table 1). The difference was largest for the topic-labelling task, where the examples slot led most participants to add labelled examples.

sections.text: The authors report that the examples slot was the most useful part of the template for most participants. They also note that several participants filled slots mechanically without understanding why each part mattered. These observations point to behaviours that a descriptive study of non-expert prompt writing could examine directly.

sections.text: A descriptive study would likely need open-ended or user-chosen tasks, multiple models, and measures such as expert ratings of prompt quality, which the authors themselves suggest. You would also need a sample and session length that reflect your target non-expert population. Piloting your own protocol before relying on the PromptScaffold design would clarify which elements actually fit your research questions.

In a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants who completed three predefined tasks, prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher automatic task score than free-form prompts (mean 0.74 vs. 0.61) and participants reported higher confidence. Structured templates are a common answer in practice, but there is little evidence on whether they help nonexperts write better prompts or only make prompts longer. This paper asks two questions. RQ1: Do prompts written with a structured template perform better on predefined tasks than free-form prompts? RQ2: How do non-expert users experience writing prompts with a template? We contribute (1) PromptScaffold, a template-based prompt editor; (2) a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants; and (3) observations on where templates help and where they constrain users. 2 Related Work Work on end-user programming shows that novices benefit from scaffolds that make implicit requirements explicit, such as forms and worked examples. Studies of prompt writing describe non-experts as relying on trial and error and on conversational phrasing. Prompt libraries and prompt-pattern catalogues offer reusable structures, but they are usually written for developers and have rarely been evaluated with non-expert users in a controlled setting. 3 The PromptScaffold Editor PromptScaffold splits a prompt into four slots. The role slot states who the model should act as.

3 The PromptScaffold Editor PromptScaffold splits a prompt into four slots. The role slot states who the model should act as. The task slot describes what to do, with a hint to name the input and the goal. The examples slot asks for one to three inputoutput pairs, and the output format slot asks how the answer should be structured. Each slot shows a short hint and an example. The editor assembles the slots into one prompt that the user can preview and edit freely before running it. A side panel shows the model's output for a small set of test inputs that the user provides. 4 Study Participants. We recruited 16 participants (9 women, 7 men, aged 19 to 27) through university mailing lists. All were undergraduate or master's students; 11 studied computing or engineering and 5 studied other subjects. None had taken a course on machine learning, and all had used a chatbot before.

8 Conclusion PromptScaffold's structured template improved task scores and confidence for non-expert users on three predefined tasks in a short lab study. sources.text: Design and tasks. The study used a within-subjects design with two conditions: free-form prompting in a plain text box, and PromptScaffold. Each participant completed three predefined tasks in each condition: classifying customer reviews by sentiment, labelling support tickets by topic, and summarising short news articles in two sentences. Condition order was counterbalanced, and parallel task versions were used so that no participant saw the same inputs twice. All prompts were run on one LLM with fixed settings. Procedure and measures. Each session lasted about 70 minutes in our lab. The main outcome was an automatic task score between 0 and 1: accuracy against gold labels for the two classification tasks and a reference-based overlap score for summaries. After each condition, participants rated their confidence in their prompts on a 7-point scale. We also recorded the time to the final prompt and held a short interview at the end of the session. 5 Results Prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher task score than free-form prompts (Table 1). The difference was largest for the topic-labelling task, where the examples slot led most participants to add labelled examples.

Designers of prompt tools for non-experts may therefore want to explain the purpose of each slot and let users drop slots that do not fit the task. 7 Limitations Our findings have three main limitations. Second, each participant used PromptScaffold in a single 70-minute lab session; we did not study long-term or real-world use, and novelty may have raised confidence.
